titre: The Nile or the Amazon: The Longest River in the World Is Not Settled
accroche: Five expeditions have proposed five different sources for the Amazon since 1969, and the Nile has fared no better.
contenu_vulgarise:
The Nile or the Amazon: which of the two is the longest river in the world? It looks like the kind of question a sufficiently precise measuring tape would settle once and for all. It isn't. For more than half a century, successive scientific expeditions have been redefining the source of the Amazon, and each redefinition changes the answer.

## The Mechanism

In 1969, the Peruvian geographer Carlos Peñaherrera del Águila is the first to propose a precise source: the Carhuasanta stream, which tumbles down Nevado Mismi in southern Peru. In 1971, the American explorer Loren McIntyre, funded by the National Geographic Society, chooses instead a small lake on the north slope of the same peak. In 1996-1997, an Italian-Peruvian expedition led by Jacek Pałkiewicz and Zaniel Novoa Goicochea rejects this lake and points to a neighboring source, beneath a rock wall on Nevado Choquecorao, judging the Apacheta stream longer than the Carhuasanta. In 1999-2000, a Czech team led by Bohumír Janský goes back to the Carhuasanta, with new measurements of the watershed. In 2014, the researchers James Contos and Nicholas Tripcevich publish in the journal Area GPS and satellite data that move the source once again: it would lie in the Cordillera Rumi Cruz, in the Mantaro River basin, 75-92 kilometers farther upstream than Nevado Mismi.

Five different identifications in forty-five years, each a little farther upstream than the last: it is not that the earlier teams made mistakes through carelessness, it is that the question “where does the Amazon begin?” has no single answer. A river is born from the confluence of thousands of streams; deciding which one counts as the “main” source requires a criterion (flow, length, basin size), and these criteria do not always point to the same stream. The same uncertainty affects the mouth: a large river that empties into the ocean through a delta splits into several channels, and the total length depends on which channel you choose to follow to the sea.

## The Shift

The common assumption is that a sufficiently precise instrument would be enough to close the debate, as was done for the height of Everest. But the length of a river is not a physical quantity fixed once and for all that remains to be measured with better tools: it is a convention, which depends on a human choice about what counts as the start and the end of the watercourse. Two honest geographers, equipped with the same satellites, can legitimately report two different lengths for the same river, because they have not chosen the same starting stream.

This is why the Nile-Amazon ranking remains disputed rather than settled, and the uncertainty is not unique to the Amazon. The Nile, long measured from Lake Victoria, has also had its most remote source redefined around the turn of the 2000s: it is now tied to the Rukarara stream, in Nyungwe Forest, in Rwanda, which brings its commonly cited length to 7,088 kilometers. No international body arbitrates which of the two rivers should be called the longest: each of them grows longer, river by river and expedition by expedition, as the chosen source recedes into the hills. The longest river in the world remains, by nature, a question of definition rather than a question of measurement.

repere.texte: In 2014, a GPS and satellite study moved the most remote source of the Amazon 75 to 92 km farther upstream than Nevado Mismi, to the Cordillera Rumi Cruz, in the Río Mantaro basin: the fifth relocation of this source since 1969.
repere.source: Contos & Tripcevich, “Correct placement of the most distant source of the Amazon River in the Mantaro River drainage”, Area, vol. 46, no. 1, 2014

carte.punch: Nile or Amazon, which is longer? The Amazon's source has been designated five times since 1969.
carte.idee: Since 1969, the source of the Amazon has been identified five times, most recently in 2014, 75-92 km farther upstream than Nevado Mismi. The Nile had its most remote source redefined around 2000, in Rwanda. The length of a river is not a fixed measurement: it is a choice about its starting point.

quiz.question: Why does the ranking of the world's longest rivers (Nile, Amazon) still change today?
choix: Because the flow of the two rivers varies so much from year to year that their length changes with the seasons
Because a river's source is not a fixed point: it depends on the criterion chosen to designate which upstream stream counts as the starting point
Because current satellites remain too imprecise to measure a river to within 1,000 km
Because political borders change regularly and redraw the official course of both rivers
quiz.explication: The length of a river depends on a human choice (which upstream stream counts as the “main” source, which delta channel counts as the mouth) and not on a lack of instrument precision; seasonal flow and political borders change nothing about the distance traveled.
